chap_01.title: The Cipher on the Tide
chap_01.summary: Silas Vance receives the stopped pocket watch at his gas-lit agency during an October gale.
chap_01.content:
The rain fell against the leaded panes of 14 High Quay Street with the persistence of a dying pulse.

Silas Vance adjusted the brass desk lamp, the wick sputtering as a draft slipped beneath the heavy oak door. Before him lay a couriers parcel—rough butcher paper, bound with tarred hemp string, smelling unmistakably of brine and dead kelp.

He slit the twine with his silver folding knife.

Inside rested an antique pocket watch. Its heavy silver casing had been blackened by sea salt, the crystal cracked diagonally from the Roman numeral nine to four. The hands were seized at precisely 3:17. When Silas pried the rear casing open with the tip of his thumbnail, no pendulum hummed. Instead, engraved into the balance cock was a single word, cut with precision: REVERIE.

Tucked behind the escapement was a folded strip of parchment, stiffened by seawater. It bore no signature—only six lines written in iron gall ink, and a wax seal stamped with the three-headed raven of House Blackwood.

If you value what remains of the harbor, Vance, do not let Alistair light the maritime lantern tonight.

Silas stood, reaching for his wool overcoat and the Webley revolver in the top drawer. Ravenscar had buried many things beneath its cold cliffs, but tonight, the tide was coughing them back up.

Every detail of the surroundings seemed etched with quiet menace. The damp sea air clung to the stone walls, condensing into slow, bead-like droplets that trailed downward like silent tears. In the distance, the foghorn sounded at deliberate four-minute intervals—a mournful iron groan that echoed across the jagged headland.

chap_02.title: The Shadows of Blackwood Manor
chap_02.summary: Silas confronts Lord Alistair Blackwood in his portrait gallery while inspecting the missing lady locked quarters.
chap_02.content:
Blackwood Manor stood upon the jagged headland like a vulture perched over a carcass.

Lord Alistair Blackwood received Silas in the grand conservatory, where dying orchids hung in humid iron cages. Alistair was a man constructed of sharp angles and nervous habit, his fingers perpetually fidgeting with a heavy gold signet ring.

My sister was hysterical, Vance. Prone to nighttime wanderings, Alistair said, pouring amber port into two cut-crystal glasses without offering one. She took a boat. A tragic accident of grief.

Hysterical women rarely mail stopped watches with coordinates to investigators four hours before they disappear, My Lord, Silas replied softly, producing the silver timepiece from his coat pocket.

Alistairs hand shook. A single droplet of dark wine spilled onto the marble floor.

Where did you get that? His voice dropped an octave, all veneer of aristocratic composure stripped clean. She kept that locked in the family reliquary. The key was buried with our father.

Silas watched the lords eyes dart toward the grand grandfather clock at the end of the gallery. For a split second, Silas noticed something strange: the clocks brass pendulum was not swinging, yet a rhythmic metallic clicking echoed from behind the mahogany wainscoting.

chap_03.title: The Whispering Archives
chap_03.summary: Silas consults archivist Clara Moreau to translate the occult sigils and discover the hidden sea vault.
chap_03.content:
The Municipal Archives smelled of vinegar, dust, and decaying leather.

Clara Moreau laid the parchment beneath a heavy brass magnifying lens, her spectacles reflecting the yellow glow of three tallow candles. Her finger traced the ravens crest, tracing down to the microscopic script hidden within the feather flourishes.

This is not Victorian cipher, Silas, Clara murmured, her voice breathless. It is fourteenth-century maritime code. The Order of the Iron Tide.

The smugglers?

Smugglers do not build underground vaults seventy fathoms into granite cliffs, she countered, sliding an ancient harbor survey across the scarred table. Look here. In 1842, the Blackwood family financed the construction of the north breakwater. On paper, it was to protect merchant vessels. But the excavation records show six hundred tons of stone were hauled out of the reef, not deposited.

She looked up at Silas, her eyes wide with dread.

Whatever was sealed beneath Ravenscar was never meant to be opened from the sea. It was meant to be unlocked from the manors cellar.

allisrar saiid fuck you


The silence that followed was swallowed by the cavernous gloom of the stacks, thick with the scent of damp lime and decaying calfskin. 

Then came the sharp, singular strike of an iron-ferruled cane against the flagstones.

From the yawning shadows between the towering shelves of parish registers, Lord Alistair Blackwood stepped into the amber ring of candlelight. His greatcoat was damp with sea mist, the velvet collar dusted with brine, but his posture bore the rigid, predatory elegance of a man who held the deed to the very ground beneath their feet. In his leather-gloved left hand, he held a salt-blackened pocket watch, its hands forever locked at seventeen minutes past three.

"You presume far too much upon the dead, Miss Moreau," Blackwood said, his voice quiet, cultured, and laced with absolute contempt. "And you meddle in ledgers that do not belong to you."

Silas moved instinctively, shifting his shoulder to shield Clara, his hand slipping toward the heavy iron paperweight on the scarred oak table. "The archives are municipal property, my Lord. Even the Blackwood reach ends at the town line."

"The Blackwood reach built the breakwater you so clumsily scrutinize," Alistair murmured, closing the distance with measured, unhurried steps. The cane came to rest upon the harbor survey, the brass tip pinning the map precisely over the excavated reef. "Six hundred tons of stone, hauled out by lantern light in the freeze of forty-two. You think it an outrage of engineering? A smuggler's bolt-hole?"

His gaze lifted, cold and pale as winter sleet, locking onto Clara behind her brass spectacles. 

"The Order did not hollow that granite to hide brandy, girl. They built a cradle. They carved a throat through which the sleeper might be fed when the tide retreats to its lowest ebb." Blackwood leaned forward slightly, the faint, metallic scent of dried blood and sea-drift clinging to his lapels. "The winter solstice is four days hence. The Blackwood debt will be settled in blood and bone, as it was written, or Ravenscar will slide into the bay and take every wretched soul in this harbor with it."

He tapped the watch face against the oak table—three deliberate, rhythmic raps.

"You have deciphered the map, but you do not hold the word. You possess the time, but not the vessel. So take your pedantic dread and choke on it. Step away from the table, Moreau, or Silas will not leave this basement on his own two feet."

chap_d4ff55d7c1.title: The Cipher on the Threshold
chap_d4ff55d7c1.content:
The story of the last man story commences in howrah  during 2150.He has a friend saptarshi whom he loved very much.



The charcoal wool of his overcoat grew heavy with the radioactive mist that clung to the skeletal remains of the Howrah grand terminus. Julian Calder adjusted his steel-framed spectacles, the glass catching the sickly, phosphorescent green of a dead railway signal that still flickered against the perpetual twilight of 2150. Beneath the iron ribs of the vaulted roof, where Victorian wrought-iron met the corroded titanium struts of a forgotten century, the silence was not merely an absence of sound. It was an accumulation. It weighed upon the chest like wet earth.

He knelt beside a rusted luggage trolley, his gloved fingers tracing the frost-rimed nameplate of his departed friend. *Saptarshi.* 

The name lived only in the grain of Julian’s memory now, as scarce as unpoisoned water. They had built the makeshift distillation rig together three winters ago, back when the coal dust from the old yards still tasted of soot rather than ash. Saptarshi had possessed a laugh like dry leaves scraping over flagstones—sharp, ephemeral, and entirely gone from the earth. Julian closed his eyes for a fraction of a second, feeling the precise, hollow contour of that loss. There was no theatrical wailing left in him; the world had burned away such luxuries long ago. There was only the methodical accounting of ghosts.

Rising with cautious stiffness, Julian reached into the reinforced inner pocket of his coat. His fingers brushed the cold, familiar brass of the private telegraph key—a relic he had salvaged from the telegraph office before the cables went permanently dead. It was his anchor to a phantom network, a piece of dead technology he wired to nothingness every midnight, just to feel the mechanical click beneath his thumb and pretend that someone, somewhere across the desolate silt of the dried Hooghly River, might still be listening.

Ahead of him, the concourse opened into the vast, echoing shadow of the main hall. A single flicker of amber light caught his eye—not the green decay of the automated signals, but something organic, warm, and utterly impossible. 

Julian’s hand drifted toward the revolver tucked at his belt, his hawk-like features tightening into an expression of grim, unsentimental resolve. In a world where he was supposed to be the final living breath, an ember in the dark was either a hallucination born of lingering coal-fumes or a trap. He stepped forward into the gloom, his boots crunching softly upon a carpet of oxidized brass filings, ready to face whatever remained of humanity—or whatever had come to finish it.

The amber glow pulsed twice, a dying heartbeat synchronized with the erratic stutter of Julian’s own pulse beneath his ribs. 

He moved with the practiced stealth of a man who had long since learned to treat his own shadow as a liability. The air inside the concourse tasted of scorched copper and damp masonry—the universal bouquet of the drowned century. Below the skeletal archways, the Hooghly basin was nothing more than a serpentine scar of cracked silt and bleached ballast stone, dividing the corpse of Calcutta from the iron ribs of Howrah where Julian stood sentinel. 

As he neared the pillar of rusted girders from whence the light emanated, the smell shifted. Beneath the metallic rot came the unmistakable tang of burning paraffin and scorched wool. 

A shadow shifted against the fluted iron of Column 42.

Julian’s boot heel locked against the grating, his weight settling instantly into his hips. He did not call out. In the year 2150, questions were acoustic suicide; if something breathed in the dark, it already knew he was there. Instead, he drew the heavy Colt navy revolver from his belt with absolute, terrifying economy of motion. The oiled metal made no sound against his woolens.

"Step out," Julian said. His voice was lower than the grinding of the distant tide-gates—a dry, rasping instrument unused to conversation, yet steady enough to cut through the vault's hollow acoustics. "Slowly. Hands where the lantern catches them."

The amber light wavered. For a heartbeat, the only response was the wet drip of radioactive condensate somewhere in the rafters above, measuring out the seconds like a leaking clock.

Then, a figure detached itself from the gloom. 

It was small, draped in layers of stiff, salt-caked canvas and grease-blackened canvas scavenged from old river barges. A knitted woolen scarf, moth-eaten and dark with age, was wound tight around the lower half of the face, but the eyes above it—wide, bloodshot, and burning with a feverish, animal panic—fixed instantly upon Julian’s spectacles. 

In the pale, sickly halo of the hand-rigged storm lantern, the stranger’s gaze did not hold the vacant stare of the feral scavengers who sometimes drifted down from the northern wastes. It held recognition. 

The figure's gloved hand trembled, lifting the lantern an inch higher. With agonizing slowness, mittened fingers reached up to unknot the heavy wool at the throat. The scarf fell away, revealing chapped, bleeding lips and a jagged scar running from jaw to ear. 

Julian’s breath caught in his throat, a sharp, metallic pain tearing at his lungs. 

It was a face he had consigned to the dirt three winters ago—a face he had buried beneath a cairn of slag-iron by the riverbank while the rain turned the ash to grey grease. 

*Saptarshi.*

The lips parted, trembling beneath the weight of a voice that had no business existing in a world emptied of echoes. 

"You're late, Calder," Saptarshi rasped, his voice like dry leaves scraping over flagstones. "I've been waiting by the wires for an hour."

The revolver remained leveled at the center of Saptarshi’s chest, its iron barrel a rigid line dividing the impossible from the real. Julian’s hand did not shake—not because he was entirely devoid of shock, but because the cold discipline of survival had become his skeleton. Yet behind the steel-rimmed spectacles, his pupils dilated in the amber glare. 

"You're in the ground," Julian said, the words slipping out of him like dry air escaping a punctured lung. "I poured the slag over you. I watched the river take the bank."

Saptarshi let out a dry, rasping sound—the phantom leaf-scrape of a laugh that Julian had cataloged among the dead. The resurrected man lowered the lantern slightly, casting long, skeletal shadows across the riveted iron floor. 

"Slag is a poor keeper, Julian," Saptarshi murmured, shifting his weight with a wince that bespoke real, aching muscle and bone. "And the river has changed its mind about who it keeps."

Before Julian could demand the impossible accounting of how a corpse had walked its way back out of the silt, a third presence stirred from the deep recess behind the pillar. 

The darkness there detached itself with the slow, deliberate creak of old leather and oiled canvas. A tall, stooped silhouette emerged from the gloom, leaning heavily upon a brass-shod walking staff. The newcomer stepped into the amber circle of the lantern, revealing a face deeply crosshatched with the geography of eighty hard years, crowned by a greasy astrakhan cap pulled low over one blind, milky eye. 

It was Lullu Dickwala. 

Lullu adjusted the heavy copper chronometer that swung from his waistcoat, tapping its glass face with a blackened thumbnail as if checking the punctuality of the resurrection.

"He talks too much, Calder," Lullu rasped, his voice like grinding millstones, rich with the sour-mash tang of fermented palm-sap and old coal. His good eye—sharp and yellowed as amber resin—fixed upon Julian with an unblinking, methodical scrutiny. "I told him to wait in the dark until the signals cleared, but the boy always had an itch for conversation. Just like his mother. Or what was left of her before the boiler burst at the central works."

Julian’s gaze flicked from Saptarshi’s living breath to Lullu’s ancient, unmoving form. The cold weight of the telegraph key in his coat pocket suddenly felt heavy, like a loaded die.

"You knew," Julian said, his voice dropping an octave, flat and lethal. 

Lullu didn't flinch. He merely leaned a fraction heavier on his staff, the brass tip clicking sharply against the oxidized brass filings beneath his boot. 

"I knew the wires across the Hooghly didn't hum by themselves three nights ago," Lullu replied, a thin, yellowed smile cracking the stubble of his jaw. "And I knew a ghost doesn't leave boot-tracks in fresh radioactive ash. You aren't the only one who refuses to let a good memory rot in the dirt, Julian. But if we're going to keep playing at being the last men on earth, you'd best lower that iron before the listening posts up at the fort catch the reflection in your lenses."

Before Julian could lower the barrel of his Colt, a sharp, theatrical gasp echoed from the deeper shadows behind Lullu’s stooped frame, accompanied by the unmistakable rustle of fine, unspotted silk—an impossible luxury in the sulfurous rot of 2150. 

A figure stepped into the sickly amber halo of the lantern, brushing past Lullu’s greasy astrakhan coat with an exaggerated, shuddering shudder of distaste. 

It was Sagnik. 

Draped in a remarkably well-preserved crimson velvet overcoat that defied the surrounding decay, Sagnik flicked a speck of invisible ash from his lapel with manicured, unblemished fingers. His sharp, heavily lined eyes swept over Julian with immediate, acidic disdain, before instantly softening into a pool of wet, unbridled adoration the moment they landed upon Saptarshi. 

"Oh, thank the heavens," Sagnik drawled, his voice a dripping, nasal honey that cut right through the hollow acoustics of the Howrah terminus. He placed a gloved hand dramatically over his heart, fluttering his eyelashes in a performance of supreme, catty exhaustion. "Put that dreadful, heavy metal thing away, Julian, you absolute Neanderthal. You’re giving us both wrinkles, and frankly, the atmosphere in this subterranean tomb is catastrophic for my complexion."

Julian’s hawk-like gaze snapped toward the newcomer, his mind—trained on the rigid calculus of survival—temporarily short-circuiting at the sheer, unfiltered absurdity of the intrusion. 

Sagnik didn't wait for an invitation. He glided past Julian’s shoulder with a sharp whiff of expensive, pre-collapse French lavender, entirely ignoring the leveled revolver. He immediately threw his arms around Saptarshi’s neck, burying his face into the damp, salt-caked canvas of the survivor's shoulder with a theatrical, trembling sigh. 

"My poor, bruised darling," Sagnik cooed, his voice shifting instantly into a syrupy, whining purr as he looked up at Saptarshi with heavy-lidded, unabashed devotion. "I told you waiting in the drafty dark for this brooding fossil would ruin your hair. If you catch a chill in this radioactive bog, I swear I will personally strangle Calder with his own telegraph wire. Didn't I tell you? Didn't I say he'd be standing here pointing guns like a tedious little peasant?"

Saptarshi winced slightly beneath the embrace, coughing into his fist, though a faint, weary fondness twitched at the corner of his chapped lips. "Sagnik, for God's sake, keep your voice down. The automated signal posts—"

"Let them listen!" Sagnik snapped, tossing his head back with a sharp, bitchy flash of his eyes as he cast a venomous glance back at Julian. "Let every rusting automaton in 2150 hear how desperately I adore you, Saptarshi, because clearly *some* people around here"—he shot a glaring, sideways look at Julian’s steel-framed spectacles—"have zero appreciation for romance, aesthetics, or the delicate nuances of gay despair in a dying world."

Lullu let out a low, gravelly chuckle from beneath his cap, leaning heavily on his brass-shod staff. "I told him to stay behind the crates," Lullu rasped, shaking his head. "He spent half the march from Calcutta complaining about the mud staining his boots."

Julian stood frozen, the cold iron of the revolver still resting in his hand, looking from the ancient, unblinking Lullu, to the supposedly dead Saptarshi, and finally to Sagnik, who was currently busy tenderly smoothing down the lapels of Saptarshi's grease-blackened coat with aggressive, possessive affection. The illusion of being the last man on earth hadn't just shattered; it had been hijacked by a bitter, bickering domestic farce.

The dry, metallic snap of a hammer coming to full cock tore through the bickering silence like a thrown stone through thin glass. 

It did not come from Julian’s Colt. 

Julian’s hawk-like eyes snapped away from Sagnik’s velvet coat, his gaze piercing the amber gloom toward the high, rusted iron catwalks that spanned the skeletal ribbing of the Howrah terminus. There, perched above the damp masonry like a gargoyle carved from coal-smoke and malice, stood Soumik. 

The silhouette was unmistakable—lean, feral, and wrapped in a tattered greatcoat that fluttered in the draft of the dead railway vault. In Soumik’s gloved fist, an old service-pattern rifle was leveled downward, the black mouth of its barrel gleaming with a lethal, oily sheen in the sickly green phosphorescence of the automated signals. 

"Stop your prattling, Sagnik," Soumik’s voice dropped from the rafters, flat, hollow, and devoid of any human warmth, ringing with the terrifying finality of a falling guillotine. "The noise brings the rot-hounds down from the north."

Sagnik froze mid-gesture, his manicured fingers arrested halfway through smoothing Saptarshi’s collar. His theatrical pout curdled instantly into a mask of pure, acid panic. "Soumik, don't be absurd, put that crude thing away—we were just—"

A sharp, deafening crack split the vaulted air. 

The report of the rifle didn't merely echo; it battered against the wrought-iron beams, shaking loose a cascade of radioactive flakes and grey soot that dusted the cracked ballast stones. 

Sagnik’s breath hitched in a high, choked whistle. The crimson velvet of his overcoat blossomed into a dark, spreading stain across his chest, right where his hand had rested a heartbeat before. He staggered backward, his heavily lined eyes widening in a grotesque parody of disbelief, before his knees buckled and he collapsed into the oxidized brass filings with the lifeless weight of a discarded bundle of rags. 

"Sagnik!" Saptarshi screamed, the sound tearing raw and ragged from his chapped throat. He lunged forward, dropping his storm lantern—the glass shattering in a starburst of amber fire and spilling burning paraffin across the floor. 

Before Saptarshi could reach the fallen velvet heap, a second dry, concussive roar detonated from the catwalk. 

The impact lifted Saptarshi off his boots. A spray of dark, arterial mist caught the dying amber light as Saptarshi slammed backward against Column 42, his chest torn open by the heavy-caliber round. He slid down the fluted iron, leaving a greasy, smeared trail of crimson against the rust, his bloodshot eyes fixing on Julian’s steel-rimmed spectacles with a silent, dying plea before the light drained from them entirely.

Silence descended upon the concourse with the suddenness of a slammed vault door. The only sound was the hissing of the spilled paraffin eating into the soot and the wet, rhythmic drip of condensate from the rafters far above.

Lullu didn't run. The old man merely leaned an inch heavier upon his brass-shod staff, his single yellowed eye turning upward toward the catwalk with a slow, unimpressed calculation. 

Julian stood frozen, the Colt navy still dangling loose in his grip. The delicate, bitter domestic farce had been wiped clean in the span of two heartbeats, leaving only the cold, unyielding iron of murder and the heavy, suffocating weight of 2150. 

High above, Soumik racked the bolt of the rifle. A spent brass casing spun from the breech, tumbling through the dim air to ping softly against the concrete floor at Julian’s feet.

A heavy, rhythmic boot-fall crunched upon the iron catwalk above, followed by the metallic drag of a zinc bucket. A wet, coughing heave broke the vaulted silence before a voice rasped out from the damp rafters—flat, grating, and thick with the rancid grease of a railway soup-kitchen.

"You left the back hatch unlatched, Soumik," Mashir Chele muttered, his heavy frame heaving into view as he hauled a dripping sack of copper scrap over the rusted railing. His wide, grease-stained face was half-swathed in wet jute, his small, pig-like eyes squinting through the sulfurous haze down at the carnage below. "The salt-mist is rusting the pulleys. And stop wasting the lead on the pretty ones. We need the brass buttons off that red coat."

Soumik did not lower the barrel of his service-pattern rifle, though his hawk-like shoulders tensed beneath his tattered greatcoat. "They were making too much noise," Soumik spat back, his voice dropping into the chill gloom. "The southern pack is moving past the canal. If the hounds smell blood here, we'll be digging our own graves in the silt."

Mashir Chele spat a dark stream of betel-nut juice over the edge; it plummeted twenty feet to splatter wetly against the oxidized filings a yard from Lullu’s polished boot-tip. The old man didn't flinch, his single yellowed eye merely tracking the red stain as it soaked into the grey dust.

"Let the hounds come," Mashir Chele grunted, his thick, calloused fingers already rummaging through the pockets of his canvas apron for a rusted wire-cutter. "There's meat on the bones yet, and the coal-stoves need feeding before the frost sets in from Dum Dum."

Julian Calder did not look down at the spent brass casing rolling against his boot. His steel-framed spectacles caught the sickly phosphorescent green of the dead signal overhead, casting a cold, emerald hue across his hawk-like features as he stared at the red-stained iron of Column 42. Saptarshi was gone. The makeshift distillation rig, the dry leaf-scrape of a laugh, the three winters of surviving the sulfurous rot of 2150—all of it had been erased by the oily gleam of Soumik’s rifle. There was no theatrical wailing left in Julian, only the hollow, methodical realization that the last man on earth was now truly, irrevocably alone once more.

Lullu Dickwala stirred, his brass-shod staff grating against the oxidized filings with a sharp, metallic ring. The old man tapped his copper chronometer with a blackened thumbnail, his single amber-resin eye shifting from Saptarshi’s lifeless form to the dark pool spreading across Sagnik’s crimson velvet.

"The time," Lullu rasped, his voice like grinding millstones smelling faintly of fermented palm-sap, "has a nasty habit of running backward when you're busy mourning ghosts."

High above, Soumik racked the bolt again, the sharp metal-on-metal clack echoing off the vaulted rafters like the striking of a match in a damp cellar. "Move the bodies to the drainage trench," Soumik called down, his voice flat and devoid of human cadence. "The mist is lifting past the old water-tower. If we stay in the open, the northern scavengers won't even wait for us to cool."

Julian did not blink. His hand remained steady around the grip of the Colt navy, the metal cold against his palm, though the internal machinery of his mind had ground to a permanent, irreversible halt. Saptarshi’s lifeless head rested at an impossible angle against the rusted fluting of Column 42, his bloodshot eyes staring upward into the vaulted gloom where the automated signals still bled their green decay. The silence that followed the gunfire was heavier than the radioactive mist settling over the Howrah terminus—a suffocating, leaden vacuum that filled the spaces where a friend's voice had lived only moments before.

"Well?" Mashir Chele’s voice scraped down from the catwalk, heavy and indifferent, accompanied by the metallic rattle of zinc buckets shifting against iron. "Are we spending the night admiring the artwork, or are we stripping the buttons before the frost sets in?"

Lullu Dickwala leaned forward, his single amber-resin eye fixed upon the widening pool of crimson soaking into the oxidized brass filings. With a slow, deliberate creak of leather and bone, the old man reached down with his blackened thumbnail and tapped the glass face of his copper chronometer. 

"The boy is finished, Mashir," Lullu rasped, his voice like two millstones grinding without grain. "Even Calder isn't foolish enough to argue with lead at this distance. Though I'd wager his telegraph key is burning a hole in his pocket right about now."

Julian did not answer. He stepped forward, his boots crunching over the shattered glass of the fallen storm lantern until he stood directly before the dead weight of Saptarshi. The salt-caked canvas of the survivor's coat was already growing stiff with the damp chill rising from the dried Hooghly basin. There was no warmth left to salvage, no remaining spark of the man who had laughed like dry leaves across flagstones. The world had proven, with brutal economy, that it had no room for ghosts—or for the men who tried to keep them alive.

From above, Soumik’s boots hit the iron grating with a heavy, deliberate thud as he descended the service ladder from the catwalk. The service-pattern rifle was slung loosely across his chest, its oily barrel catching the sickly green phosphor of the dead signal. He did not look at Julian, nor did he offer a glance toward the crimson velvet heap where Sagnik lay motionless. He walked straight past Column 42, his jaw set in a hard, impassable line, and reached down to grab Saptarshi by the stiffened collar of his canvas coat.

"Help me with the legs," Soumik said, his voice flat, stripped of any inflection that might suggest regret or malice. It was simply the voice of a butcher clearing the floorboards at the end of a long shift.

Julian looked down at his own hands—gloved, steady, and entirely useless. The private telegraph key in his reinforced inner pocket gave no phantom click against his ribs; it remained as dead and silent as the wires overhead. With a grim, unsentimental economy of motion, Julian reached down, grasped Saptarshi’s boot by the frozen leather, and helped drag what remained of his only friend toward the dark mouth of the drainage trench.

chap_2900819ce6.title: Chapter 3 - The Unfolding Incident
chap_2900819ce6.content:
The cold air of the concourse tasted of damp coke-dust and old iron. Soumik’s boots dragged across the ribbed plating, the dead weight of Saptarshi’s heels leaving parallel furrows in the thick layer of soot that had settled over the floor since the great pumps failed. 

"Don't let the grit get into the joints," Soumik muttered, his breath pluming grey against the vault’s permanent twilight. His shoulders strained beneath the wet wool of his greatcoat as he heaved the upper torso past the rusted stanchion of Column 42. "Once the salt sets in the marrow, you can't even sell the bones to the grease-boilers down at Kidderpore."

Julian did not offer to take the other side. His fingers remained buried in the deep, reinforced pockets of his coat, curled tight around the cold, dead brass of the telegraph key. The metal bit into his palm, a sharp, familiar anchor against the rising tide of silence that always followed the cessation of gunfire. 

Lullu Dickwala watched them from the shadow of the pillar, his brass-shod staff planted firmly between his worn leather boots like the mast of a broken barge. His single amber-resin eye caught the sickly green phosphor of the distant signal box, reflecting the dying luminescence with an unblinking, reptilian fixity. 

"The boy was always impatient," Lullu rasped, the sound like dry leaves scraping across a frozen flagged court. He reached into his waistcoat, his blackened thumbnail clicking against the copper casing of his chronometer before letting the lid snap shut with a dull *tink*. "Thought the wires were still talking to something north of the canal. Thought there were still clerks at the junction stamping forms for the grain barges. A boy born in forty-five doesn't understand what a dead city sounds like when the rats finally clear out."

"He had papers," Julian said. His voice was flat, level, cutting through the hollow acoustics of the station with the dry precision of an autopsy report. 

"Papers won't butter a stale crust, Calder," Lullu replied, shifting his weight with a dry creak of hide and bone. "You've got a pocket full of copper and wire that hasn't ticked a true word since the governor’s barge sank off Garden Reach. You keep listening to that little box like an old woman waiting for a son who died in the trenches."

Soumik dropped Saptarshi’s boots with a dull, hollow thud against the ribbed iron. He did not step back immediately; instead, he stood over the inert canvas bundle, his chest heaving slowly under the tattered wool. His dark, hawk-like eyes flicked upward toward the high, soot-blackened rafters where the rusted remnants of the overhead cranes hung like the ribs of prehistoric leviathans. 

"The north hatch is clear," Soumik said, his voice dropping into the space between them. "The tide’s coming up the basin. If we're going to move the crate before the brackish water hits the lower conduits, we need to take it now."

Julian pulled his hand from his pocket, the telegraph key leaving a faint smudge of cold grease against the wool lining. He looked down at the dead man at his feet—at the stiffened canvas of the coat, the rimed frost forming along the edges of the unbuttoned collar, the absolute, unyielding finality of a world that refused to provide answers even to those who stayed behind to ask them. 

"The crate stays," Julian said. 

Soumik’s jaw tightened, the muscle beneath his stubbled cheek twitching once. "It’s copper-lined. We can trade the sheeting at the dock-gates for enough paraffin to last through the freeze."

"It stays," Julian repeated, his gaze lifting to meet Soumik’s unblinking stare across the dim expanse of the concourse. "And we leave Saptarshi where the iron won't wash him out with the scum."

Lullu let out a low, dry chuckle that ended in a wet, rattling cough. He turned his astrakhan cap toward the dark mouth of the drainage trench, his amber eye gleaming in the gloom. "Let the mud have him, then. The Hooghly doesn't charge for storage."

The dark mouth of the drainage trench yawned before them like an unsealed crypt, exhaling a damp, mineral-laden breath that tasted faintly of old sulfur and stagnant river-silt. Julian stepped closer to the edge, his boots crunching upon the brittle crust of oxidized filings. The steel-framed spectacles on his bridge caught the sickly, intermittent flash of the green signal-lamp overhead, throwing two emerald arcs across the planes of his hollow cheeks.

"A sentimental journey for a dead clerk," Soumik muttered, his fingers hooking into the stiff collar of Saptarshi’s canvas coat with careless familiarity. With a sudden, synchronized heave, Soumik and Lullu—whose brass-shod staff clicked sharply against the iron plates—dragged the inert bundle toward the drop. 

There was no ceremony, no whispered liturgy for the end of days. In Howrah, 2150, death was merely a shift in inventory. 

Saptarshi’s shoulder struck the wet brickwork of the trench lining with a dull, hollow *thump*, followed immediately by the heavier, wet slide of limbs slipping into the dark mire below. A small cloud of grey, phosphorescent scum bubbled to the surface of the brackish water, winked once in the dim air, and vanished. 

Julian did not look down into the trench. Instead, his hand slipped back into the deep, reinforced pocket of his charcoal wool overcoat, finding the cold, familiar contours of the telegraph key. His thumb traced the brass stud, feeling the microscopic ridges where a thousand telegrams had once been hammered out across a continent that no longer breathed. 

"The northern pack is moving," Soumik said, wiping his grease-stained palm across his thigh as he straightened his back. His dark eyes remained fixed on the cavernous shadows stretching toward the old platform gates. "Mashir Chele won't wait long by the cranes. If we're going to check the wire-vaults beneath the ticket office before the tide backs up through the culverts, we need to move now."

Lullu Dickwala let out a dry, rasping breath, his single amber-resin eye reflecting the green phosphor with predatory indifference. He tapped his copper chronometer against his blackened thumbnail, the metallic click sharp and lonely in the hollow vault. 

"The boy left his key in the pocket," Lullu murmured, his voice like grinding stone. He tilted his astrakhan cap toward Julian. "The one from the central loop. He swore he heard the relay clicking two nights ago, right before the substation went dark."

Julian’s fingers tightened around the metal in his pocket until the edges bit into his palm. The world outside these soot-stained iron ribs was a graveyard of drowned barges and rusted rails, a silent monument to the last man delusion that he and his companions lived within. But down here, in the damp, rotting belly of the station, the wires still remembered names that the earth had forgotten.

"It wasn't the central loop," Julian said quietly, his voice cutting through the drip of condensate like a dry blade. "It was the loop to Dum Dum."

"Then let's see if anyone's answering," Soumik said, turning his back on the drainage trench and gripping the service-pattern rifle in his gloved fist. He didn't wait for agreement, his heavy boots splashing faintly as he stepped toward the rusted archway of the subterranean stairs. 

Julian lingered for a fraction of a second longer, his eyes casting one final, lingering look at the dark, oily surface of the water where Saptarshi had disappeared. Then, with the grim, unsentimental economy of a man who knew the dead never wrote back, he turned and followed the sound of iron boots into the dark.

chap_1cc2c532c9.title: Press Start
chap_1cc2c532c9.content:
Sougat apne room ke andheray mein, sirf RGB keyboard ki blue aur red glow ke sahare, monitor screen ke samne baitha tha. Ek haath mein mouse aur dusre se chipka hua chai ka cup, jo abhi tak thanda bhi nahi hua tha. 

"Bhai, ye match firse haar gaye toh kasam se game delete kar dunga," Sougat ne headpiece mic ke paas apna muh laate hue kaha.

Dusri taraf se Saptarshi ki aawaz aayi, jo apni chair par stretch karte hue headset adjust kar raha tha. "Arre Sougat bhai, tu har baar yahi bolta hai aur agle ghante rank push karne lagta hai. Tera 'delete' wala threat mere 90 FPS wale PC jitna hi fake hai!"

Sougat ne screen par apna inventory check kiya. 2026 ke is naye multiplayer tactical shooter mein, unka squad wahi haar ke kabaar mein khada tha. "Saptarshi, tu has mat. Meri coding aur tera aim—dono aajkal ekdum dhoka de rahe hain. Pata nahi kab sudhrenge."

Saptarshi haste hue bola, "Coding toh fir bhi fix ho jaati hai bhai, tere ye noob wale reflex kaise fix honge? Ek kaam kar, paani peeke aa, thoda brain cell reboot kar le."

Sougat ne screen par dekha jahan Saptarshi ka character uske virtual avatar ke paas aakar emote maar raha tha. Dil se toh dono ek dusre ko gaali hi de rahe the, par gaming ke is endless loop mein yehi toh unka apna heartwarming bromance tha. 

"Ruk abhi, agla round tera bhai hi carry karega," Sougat ne confidence se bolte hue 'Ready' button par click kiya.

"Carry karega? Bhai, pehle ye toh dekh le ki tu grenade phekne ke chakkar mein khud ke character ko hi uda deta hai," Saptarshi ne mic par ek thakha hua par pyaar bhara thahaka lagaya. 

Sougat ne chai ka aakhri ghoont bhara, cup table par patak diya aur mouse par apni grip mazboot ki. Uske room ki deewaron par blue aur red LED lights ka reflection aise nach raha tha jaise unka yeh 2026 ka naya-naya game unke mood ke sath khel raha ho. Bahar gali mein kisi scooter ka horn baja, par unke liye duniya ka aakhri kona bas yeh 24-inch ka monitor hi tha.

"Chal, is baar no mistakes. Tu bas peeche se cover dena, aur haan, agar is baar bhi mara na, toh chai ki treat teri taraf se hogi," Sougat ne shart lagate hue kaha.

Saptarshi muskurate hue apne 90 FPS rig par mouse glide karne laga. "Manzoor hai! Par treat jeetne ke baad bhi khayega toh tu hi, kyunki teri bhookh ka koi ant nahi hai."

Lobby ka countdown shuru ho chuka tha—3, 2, 1... Aur uss chote se screen ke samne baithe dono dost ek baar phir us digital jung mein कूद pade, jahan haar aur jeet se zyada zaroori yeh hansi aur dosti thi jo is adhi raat ko bhi roshan kar rahi thi.

Map load hote hi screen par synthetic aawazon ka shor goonj utha. Sougat ne apna headpiece mic thoda aur paas kiya, saansein rokte hue apne virtual character ko ek industrial corridor ke kone mein chupaya. 

"Dekh Saptarshi, is baar main flank kar raha hoon. Tu seedha middle gate se entry le aur dhyaan rakhna, pichli baar ki tarah kisi corner mein atak mat jaana," Sougat ne thode hoshiyaari wale tone mein kaha, jabki uske khud ke haath mouse par tharthara rahe the.

Saptarshi apne 90 FPS PC par screen ke smooth framerates ka fayda uthate hue bina kisi delay ke aage badha. "Bhai, mera movement मक्खन jaisa hai, tu bas apne footstep check kar. Aise chal raha hai jaise paanv mein chappal pehen ke sniper map mein utar aaya ho."

"Chup kar, noob," Sougat hansa, aur screen par apne character ko aage badhaya. 

Lekin jaise hi unka squad map ke center ki taraf badha, saamne se enemy team ke do players ne achanak dhawa bol diya. Goliyon ki tarah aawazein aur flashbangs ki chamak se unka monitor jagmagane laga. 

"Arre bhai! Aage bomb hai, aage bomb—" Sougat chillaya, aur panic mein aakar keyboard par galat key dabagayi. Uska character seedha ek deewar se takra kar ruk gaya aur wahi freeze ho gaya. 

Saptarshi ne turant react karte hue apne character ko enemy ke line of fire ke beech khada kiya aur ek perfect headshot ke sath pehle dushman ko dharti par gira diya. "Bhai, tu sach mein disaster management ka brand ambassador hai! Ek toh tu khud fass jata hai, upar se mera bhi dhyan bhatka deta hai."

Sougat ne sharminda hote hue screen par dekha jahan uska character abhi bhi corner mein chupne ki naakam koshish kar raha tha. Usne thandi ho chuki chai ki taraf dekha aur phir monitor par. "Arre, strategy thi wo! Enemy ko confuse karne ki high-level tactical move... tu nahi samjhega."

"Haan bhai, itni high-level ki ab agla round shuru hote hi mujhe hi tujhe revive karna padega," Saptarshi ne mic par muskurate hue kaha, uski aawaz mein wohi purana dostana mazak tha jo kisi bhi haar ko hansi mein badal deta tha.

Round khatam hone ka buzzer baja, aur screen par 'Defeat' ka bada sa red font chamka. 

Sougat ne zor se apna sir desk par maara, par ek hi second baad woh khilkhila kar hans pada. "Chal, koi baat nahi. Agli baar pakka jeetenge. Par abhi ke liye... tera chai ki treat ka wada pakka raha, kyunki shart toh main hi haar gaya."

Saptarshi ne apne headset ko adjust karte hue jawab diya, "Chal thik hai, kal subah tapri wali chai teri taraf se, bas aaj game mat delete karna."

RGB lights ki wohi blue aur red roshni abhi bhi unke kamron mein chamak rahi thi, aur adhi raat ke is sannate mein dosti ka yeh silsila bina kisi interruption ke agle match ki loading screen ki taraf badh chuka tha.

Loading screen ke gayab hote hi lobby ke naye match ki aawaz goonj uthi, par is baar dono doston ke beech ka virtual fasla jaise pal bhar ke liye gayab ho gaya kyunki unke agle kadam ne unhe screen ke aar-paar aamne-samne la khada kiya tha. Sougat ne apne headpiece mic ko thoda aur theek kiya, apni chair ko desk ke thoda aur kareeb kheencha, aur computer screen ke 24-inch glass ke doosri taraf baithe Saptarshi ki virtual aankhon mein dekhte hue ek baar phir challenge feka. 

"Ruk Saptarshi, abhi screen ke is paar aur tere 90 FPS ke uss paar ka hisaab barabar karte hain," Sougat ne muskurate hue kaha, jabki blue aur red RGB lights ka noor unke chehron par ek alag hi rang bikher raha tha. 

Saptarshi ne apne headset ko ek taraf sirkaate hue screen ke samne se halka sa leaning posture banaya, maano woh sach mein Sougat ki aankhon mein dekh raha ho. "Bhai, pehle apni coding aur reflexes theek kar le, warna agla match bhi wahi 'Defeat' wale red board par khatam hoga aur chai ki treat toh waise bhi teri hi jeb se jaani hai!" 

Adhi raat ke uss sannate mein, game ki digital duniyan aur haqeeqat ke beech ka woh pal ek aisi hansi mein doob gaya, jahan haar aur jeet se kahin zyada gehra unka yeh 2026 ka unmatchable bromance chamak raha tha.

Loading screen ke gayab hote hi lobby ke naye match ki aawaz goonj uthi, par is baar unke samne koi random bots nahi, balki do aise naye khiladi the jinhone poori lobby ka mood hi badal diya tha—Soumik aur Sagnik. 

Sougat ne screen par unke usernames dekhte hi apne headpiece mic ko thoda aur theek kiya, apni chair ko desk ke thoda aur kareeb kheencha. "Arre dekh, yeh Soumik aur Sagnik kaun naye nishanebaaz aa gaye hain match mein? Lagta hai aaj inhi se muqabla hai."

Saptarshi ne apne 90 FPS rig par mouse glide karte hue screen ke samne se halka sa leaning posture banaya. "Bhai, Soumik aur Sagnik toh wahi hain jo pichle tournament mein bhi gandi tarah haar kar gaye the. Inhe kya pata ki humare samne tikna kitna mushkil hai!"

Dusri taraf se, match ke chat box aur voice channel mein Soumik aur Sagnik ki awazein gunj uthi. Soumik ne haste hue mic par kaha, "Oye Sougat aur Saptarshi! Bahut bade pro ban rahe ho na? Aaj tum dono ko aisa dhul chataenge ki game delete karne ki zaroorat hi nahi padegi, seedha PC hi bechna padega!"

Sagnik ne turant uski haan mein haan milate hue apna character aage badhaya. "Sahi bola Soumik! Inka 90 FPS aur coding ka ghamand aaj yeh Soumik aur Sagnik mil kar todne wale hain. Tayyar ho jao haar ke liye, Sougat bhai!"

Sougat ke hontho par ek confident muskurahat ubhri. Usne blue aur red RGB lights ke beech apne mouse par grip mazboot ki aur bol pada, "Accha ji? Soumik aur Sagnik bhai, pehle ye toh dekh lo ki tumhara spawn point kahan hai, warna shuru hote hi wapas lobby mein jana padega!"

Saptarshi ne bhi apne character ko cover dete hue wahi purana dosto wala mazak dohraya, "Sahi kaha Sougat! In dono ko toh aaj aisi class denge ki Soumik aur Sagnik poori zindagi tactical shooter khelna bhool jayenge."

Adhi raat ke uss sannate mein, game ki digital duniyan aur haqeeqat ke beech ka woh pal ek aisi hansi aur mukable mein doob gaya, jahan Sougat aur Saptarshi ka samna ab Soumik aur Sagnik ke sath ek romanchak aur mazedaar match mein ho chuka tha.






Round ki count-down khatam hote hi gate khul gaye, aur Sougat ne bina ek pal gavaye apne character ko sidha tactical corridor ki taraf dauda diya. 

"Dekh Saptarshi, is baar main seedha aage ja raha hoon, tu flank kar!" Sougat ne mic par thode josh aur thodi ghabrahat ke sath kaha. 

Screen ke doosri taraf se Saptarshi ki aawaz aayi, jo apne 90 FPS PC par poori focus ke sath mouse chala raha tha. "Bhai, thoda dheere chal, wahan aage Soumik aur Sagnik pehle se hi position leke baithe honge. Tu apne character ko firse kisi deewar mein mat ghusa dena!"

"Arre nahi bhai, aaj mera aim ekdum sniper jaisa hai!" Sougat ne confidence dikhate hue aage badhne ki koshish ki, par tabhi screen ke dusre kone se Soumik ka character achanak samne aa gaya aur usne dharadhar goliyan chalani shuru kar diyan. 

Voice channel mein Soumik ki hansi goonji, "Kya hua Sougat bhai? Kahan gaya tera sniper jaisa aim? Idhar dekh, Soumik tere saare confidence ki hawa nikaal raha hai!"

Sagnik ne bhi turant apna character aage badhate hue mazaakiya andaz mein chidhaaya, "Sahi pakda Soumik! Isko batao ki 2026 mein noob play kaise hota hai. Sagnik aur Soumik ki jodi se bachke rehna itna aasan nahi hai, Saptarshi bhai!"

Sougat panic mein keyboard par galat keys dabane laga. "Arre yaar, ye Soumik achanak kahan se tapak pada! Saptarshi, bacha le warna aaj firse tea treat ki naubat aa jayegi!"

Saptarshi ne bina waqt gavaye apne character ko ekdum smooth speed se enemy ke line of fire ke beech utaar diya aur Sagnik par ek perfect burst fire karke usko wahi dher kar diya. "Bhai, tu sach mein ek number ka drama queen hai! Sagnik ko toh maine gira diya, par abhi Soumik baaki hai."

Screen par Sagnik ke character ko girta dekh Soumik ki aawaz thodi dheemi padi, "Arre Sagnik bhai ko kaise gira diya! Ruko Saptarshi, ab main batata hoon."

Sougat ne sans rokte hue apni thandi ho chuki chai ke cup ko chhua aur wapas mouse par haath rakh diya. RGB lights ki neeli aur laal roshni unke kamron mein abhi bhi chamak rahi thi, aur adhi raat ke is mukable mein dosti, hansi aur game ka yeh rangin safar aur bhi romanchak ho chuka tha.




Soumik ki aawaz voice channel par thodi aur tez ho gayi, "Saptarshi bhai, abhi toh party shuru hui hai! Tu akela thodi na bachega!" 

Saptarshi ne apne headset ko thoda aur kaste hue screen par dekha, jahan Soumik ka character ab poori aagressive chaal ke saath unke virtual bunker ki taraf badh raha tha. "Bhai Sougat, tu bas corner hold karke rakh, main yeh Soumik ka game bajata hoon!" Saptarshi ne haste hue mouse par apna grip mazboot kiya, uske 90 FPS rig ki smooth screen par flashbangs ki roshni chamak uthi. 

Sougat ne apni thandi ho chuki chai ke cup ko ek taraf rakha, keyboard par ungliyan tezi se daudate hue bola, "Arre dekh kar! Piche se Sagnik bhi wapas spawn ho kar aa raha hoga, kasam se agar yeh round haar gaye na, toh chai ki treat ke sath-sath agle hafte ka bill bhi tera hi hoga!"

"Chal jhoothe!" Saptarshi ne ek dum fluid movement ke sath apne character ko side corridor mein dala aur direct Soumik ke crosshairs ke samne slide kiya. "Pehle tu apna aim theek kar le, warna agla match firse wahi 'Defeat' wale red screen par khatam hoga!"

Adhi raat ke uss sannaate mein, RGB lights ki neeli aur laal roshni ke beech, dono doston ki yeh hansi aur nok-jhok us digital jung ko aur bhi zyada roshan kar rahi thi. Haar aur jeet apni jagah thi, par is 2026 ki raat mein unka yeh unmatchable bromance kisi bhi pro-league trophy se kahin zyada keemti lag raha tha.

Soumik aur Sagnik ki baatein sunkar Sougat ne apne keyboard par ek zor ka thappad mara. "Bhai, inki overconfidence dekh raha hai? Pichli baar kya jeet gaye, khud ko Esports ka legend samajhne lage hain," Sougat ne mic par bhadakte hue kaha, jabki uske face par ek choti si muskan bhi thi. Saptarshi ne apne 90 FPS rig par screen refresh karte hue ek thanda sa smirk diya, "Inhe kya pata bhai, apna comeback hamesha sabse dangerous hota hai. Tu bas apni ungliyan sahi key par rakh, warna is baar chai ke sath samosa bhi teri hi jeb se aayega!"

Lobby ke screen par 'Match Starting' ka flashing sign aate hi dono teams ke beech ka tension ek alag hi level par pahunch gaya tha. Map load hote hi Soumik aur Sagnik ke characters ne aggressive push dena shuru kar diya. Sougat ne apne character ko ek diwar ke peeche chupate hue dheere se kaha, "Saptarshi, ye dono seedha rush kar rahe hain. Left flank se main cover deta hoon, tu middle se inka game baja de." Saptarshi bina ek bhi second waste kiye fluid motion mein aage badha, uske monitor par high frame rates ka magic saaf dikh raha tha. "Tu bas dekhta ja, bhai! Inka overconfidence hi inki sabse badi weakness banne wali hai."

Goliyon ki gaddagaddi aur footstep ki aawazon se purana tactical corridor goonj utha. Sougat ne apne daant peeshte hue mouse par grip aur kas li, uske dimag mein bas ek hi baat chal rahi thi—agar is baar Soumik aur Sagnik se haar gaye, toh poore saal bhar inke taane sunne padenge. 

"Ruk jao dono, abhi batata hoon!" Sougat ne achanak aage badhte hue ek flashbang feka, jo zid karte hue theek unki deewar par lag kar wapas uske hi paas gir pada. 

"Arre bhai! Flashbang feka tha ya apne hi pair pe kulhadi maari thi?!" Saptarshi ki cheekh mic ke zariye goonj uthi, kyunki screen par white glare fail chuka tha aur Saptarshi ka character andhepan mein idhar-udhar goli chalane laga tha. 

"Sorry, sorry! Woh key thodi slip ho gayi thi!" Sougat ne haste hue keyboard par haath patak diya, jabki screen ke uss paar se Soumik aur Sagnik ki hasne ki aawazein saaf sunayi de rahi thin. 

"Wah Sougat bhai! Kya tactical move hai! Khud ko hi blind kar liya, ab toh bas respawn ka wait hi bacha hai!" Sagnik ki aawaz mein poori tarah se teasing aur mazaak bhara hua tha. 

Lekin Saptarshi apne 90 FPS rig ki taqat aur shant dimaag ke sath abhi bhi haar maanne ke mood mein nahi tha. Screen par jaise hi flash ka asar kam hua, usne apne high-end monitor par fluid precision ke sath aim flick kiya aur ek hi second mein Soumik ke character ko headshot de kar dharti par gira diya. "Yeh le beta! Overconfidence ka trailer!" Saptarshi ne chillate hue kaha. 

Sougat, jo abhi tak apne hi flash se pareshan tha, josh mein aakar chillaya, "Bhai maardiya! Sagnik akela bacha hai, ab mat chhodna isko!" Adhi raat ke is sannate mein unka yeh gaming room ek virtual warzone se kam nahi lag raha tha, jahan dosti, gussa aur hansi ka ek anokha hi mixture bann chuka tha.

Sagnik ka character, jo achanak apne partner Soumik ke girne se thoda hichkichaya tha, turant piche hatne laga. Par Saptarshi aur Sougat kahan chhodne wale the. Sougat ne apne character ki aankhon se safed glare hatte hi keyboard par apni ungliyan tez chalaani shuru kar diin. "Ruk ja Sagnik, kahan bhaag raha hai? Abhi toh party shuru hui hai!" Sougat ne josh mein aakar table par thappad mara, jisse uska chai ka khali cup halka sa uchal gaya.

Saptarshi ne bina ek bhi second gawaye apne character ko ek pillar ke peeche se glide karate hue aage badhaya. Uske 90 FPS rig par har movement itni smooth dikh rahi thi maano koi cinematic movie chal rahi ho. "Bhai Sougat, tu is baar aage mat badh, warna tu khud ko ya mujhe firse uda dega. Main akela hi iska kaam tamam karta hoon," Saptarshi ne mic par ek confident muskan ke sath kaha.

Dusri taraf voice channel mein Sagnik ki aawaz thodi ghabrahat ke sath aayi, "Oye Saptarshi, akele-akele kahan aa raha hai? Himmat hai toh samne aakar ladiye!" Par uski yeh baatein ab sirf ek aakhri koshish lag rahi thi. Saptarshi ne screen par Sagnik ke character ki shadow dekhte hi apne mouse par ek sharp click kiya aur bina waqt zaya kiye ek clean burst fire chhod di. 

*Crack!* 

Screen par Sagnik ka character bhi dharti par dher ho gaya, aur uske turant baad poori lobby mein ek bright green font mein 'Victory' chamakne laga. 

"Bum! Khtm tata bye-bye!" Sougat ne khushi se chillate hue apni chair piche dhakel di, jisse woh piche rakhi deewar se takra gayi. Usne apne headset ko utaar kar table par rakha aur zor-zor se hansne laga. "Dekh liya Saptarshi? Kehte hain na, ant bhala toh sab bhala! Humne inka ghamand ek hi jhatke mein zameen doosj kar diya!"

Saptarshi ne apne headset ko thoda upar karte hue chain ki saans li aur apne 90 FPS keyboard par ungliyan thapthapate hue bola, "Haar-jeet toh chalti rehti hai bhai, par asli jeet ismein hai ki tera flashbang lagne ke baad bhi humne round nikal liya. Warna kal subah ki chai ki tapri wali treat mujhe hi deni padti!"

Chat box mein Soumik aur Sagnik ki taraf se ab koi gusse ya overconfidence wala message nahi aa raha tha, balki wahan sirf ek chota sa message flash hua: *"Rematch hoga kal!"* 

Sougat ne screen par us message ko dekh kar ek broad grin diya aur paas hi rakhe thande chai ke cup ko utha kar ek lamba ghoont bhara. Adhi raat ka sannata ek baar fir se unki dosti ki khilkhilahat aur agle din ki planning mein doob gaya, jahan 2026 ki is digital duniya mein unka bromance pehle se kahin zyada pakka ho chuka tha.

"Kal ka rematch toh door ki baat hai, pehle yeh bata ki agle hafte ka bill kaun bharega kyunki aaj ki is epic jeet ki khushi mein treat double ho chuki hai," Sougat ne haste hue mic mein kaha, uski aawaz mein 2026 ki is adhi raat ki thakan ki jagah ek naya hi josh daud raha tha. Saptarshi ne apne chair par stretch karte hue 90 FPS screen ki taraf dekha jahan lobby ka score board abhi bhi unki victory ka gawah ban kar chamak raha tha. "Chal bhai, treat ki baat aayi hai toh woh bhi dekh lenge, par pehle apne keyboard ko bol thoda shant rahe, warna agli baar tera flashbang seedha mere room mein aakar girega." Kamre ki neeli aur laal RGB lights ki roshni mein dono doston ki yeh hansi ek baar phir gunj uthi, aur unke beech ka yeh unmatchable bromance kisi bhi jeet ya haar se kahin zyada gehra saabit ho chuka tha.

Saptarshi ne haste hue apna headset table par theek se rakha aur chair se uthte hue angdayi li. Kamre ki thandak mein abhi bhi computer fans ki hum aur unki baaton ki goonj baaki thi. Khidki ke baahar 2026 ki is shaant raat mein halki si thandi hawa chal rahi thi, jo is garma-garam gaming session ke baad ekdum sukoon de rahi thi.

"Chal bhai Sougat, ab soney ka time ho gaya hai, warna subah tapri wali chai ke waqt teri wahi late-latif wali kahaniyan sunni padengi," Saptarshi ne mic band karte hue kaha.

Sougat ne bhi apni screen par 'Exit to Desktop' wale button par click kiya aur apne thake hue par khilkhilate hue chehre par ek jeet ki muskan liye apne cup ko table par rakh diya. "Soney ki baat mat kar Saptarshi, abhi toh dimag mein agle din ki strategy chal rahi hai. Kal jab Soumik aur Sagnik rematch ke liye aayenge, toh hum unhe bina flashbang ke hi hara denge—bas tu apni taraf se wahi 90 FPS wala magic chalate rehna."

Dono doston ki yeh halki-fulki nok-jhok aur dosti ka yeh anokha silsila adhi raat ke is aakhri pehar mein bhi waisa hi taza tha jaisa match shuru hone se pehle tha. Neeli aur laal RGB lights ki roshni dheere-dheere dim hone lagi, par unke dil aur dimaag mein is jeet ki chamak abhi bhi baaki thi. 

Kamra shant ho gaya, par 2026 ki is raat ne unke is unmatchable bromance ko ek nayi aur haseen yaad de di thi, jo kal subah ki tapri wali chai ke sath ek baar phir taza hone ke liye taiyar thi.
